name: Finding an Internship
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Run an internship search: timeline, where to look, applying well, referrals, cold messages, offers and earning a return offer.

resources.title: Handshake
resources.note: Student job board used by many universities for internship postings.

resources.title: Simplify internship listings
resources.note: Searchable internship listings with filters for role, location and season.

resources.title: NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates
resources.note: Paid summer research programs for US undergraduates.

resources.note: Free guide to negotiating offers in tech.

lesson.intro: Getting an internship is a search problem as much as a skills problem: apply at the right time, in the right places, through the right people, and keep going through rejections. This lesson covers the calendar, applying, referrals, cold messages, tracking, offers and return offers.
objectives: Plan around the fall large-company wave and the spring second wave
Apply efficiently with a tiered list, quick tailoring and strong short answers
Write short cold messages and ask for referrals the right way
Track applications and fix the weakest stage of your search
Handle offers and deadlines, and earn a return offer

sections.title: The timeline: earlier than you think
sections.key: US large companies typically open summer internship applications in late summer and early fall of the year before, reviewing on a rolling basis; smaller companies hire into spring.
sections.body:
Every year, students start looking for a summer internship in March and find that many large companies filled their programs months earlier.

In the US, large companies typically open summer applications in **late summer and early fall of the year before**, often reviewed on a **rolling basis**: interviews start as applications arrive and stop when spots fill. Apply in the first weeks.

Smaller companies and startups hire closer to the start, often in winter and spring. So there are two waves; ride both, and check each company's student careers page, since dates shift every year.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Check eligibility: most internships are for students returning to school, so forms ask for your graduation date. International students should talk to the international student office early about work authorization (in the US, F-1 students commonly use CPT) and answer form questions accurately.

visual.title: A typical US calendar
rows: May to Aug, the year before
Polish your resume, GitHub and LinkedIn; finish one or two projects; start interview practice; build a target list
Large companies typically open applications; career fairs; apply early
Online assessments, phone screens, final rounds
Offers arrive, often with decision deadlines
Second wave: mid-size companies and startups
The internship itself, often 10 to 12 weeks

visual.title: Other routes
rows: Fall or spring terms, usually with less competition
Common at some universities, often four to eight months
Run by some large companies; search "first-year internship" or "sophomore internship" in late summer
With a professor, or a summer REU (NSF-funded Research Experiences for Undergraduates): real experience too

sections.tip: Set a calendar reminder for early August. When the big postings open, you want your resume ready, not in progress.
sections.pitfall: Waiting until your resume feels perfect. With rolling review, a good resume sent in September usually beats a perfect one sent in January.

check.question: It's February and you have just started looking for a summer internship. What's the best plan?
choices: Give up on this summer, since everything is filled
Focus on startups, mid-size and local companies that hire closer to summer, and apply to any large-company postings still open
Apply only to the biggest companies, since they pay the most
Wait until next August to start
check.explanation: Many large programs fill in the fall, but the second wave of hiring (startups, mid-size companies, local and non-tech employers) runs through spring. Some large postings also stay open. Giving up or waiting wastes a whole season.

sections.title: Where to find roles
sections.key: Search widely (career pages, job boards, Handshake, community lists, fairs and less famous employers), verify every posting on the company's own site, and expect volume.
sections.body:
Most students search one job board, apply to the same 30 famous companies as everyone else, and conclude the market is impossible. Widen the net:

[[visual]]

**Less obvious employers** (banks, retailers, hospitals, government agencies, nonprofits, local companies) all hire software interns and get far fewer applicants per spot. Communities count too: hackathons, meetups, student Discord or Slack groups, conferences with student tickets.

[[visual 2]]

Expect volume: many students send dozens of applications to get a handful of interviews. That ratio is normal and not a judgment of you; referrals and well-targeted applications improve it.

visual.title: Where roles are posted
rows: You must know the company exists: keep a target list
Huge volume; alerts for "software engineer intern"
Roles aimed at students, through universities
Links go stale: confirm on the company's own site
Talk to a person, skip the pile
Go early with a 30-second pitch, printed resumes and a specific question per company

visual.title: Fake internships target students every season

items.title: Scam warning signs
points: You must pay for training or equipment
They send a check to deposit and ask you to send part back
You are hired after a text-only chat with no real interview

items.title: What to do
points: Find the posting on the company's own careers site
Contact the company through that site, not the message you got

sections.tip: Keep a target list of 40 to 80 companies across tiers: famous, mid-size, startups and local. It stops you from refreshing one job board all day.
sections.pitfall: Applying only to the most famous companies. They get the most applicants per spot, while mid-size and non-tech companies often offer great first internships with much better odds.

check.question: You found an internship on a community GitHub list. What should you do before applying?
choices: Apply through the list's link without checking
Email the list's maintainer and ask for a referral
Open the posting on the company's own careers site to confirm it is real, still open and a fit
Skip it, since community lists are never accurate
check.explanation: Community lists are a great discovery tool, but links go stale and postings close. The company's careers page is the source of truth for whether the role is open and what it requires. Maintainers curate links; they don't refer applicants.

sections.title: Applying well: timing, tiers and short answers
sections.key: Apply early to a tiered list, spend about five minutes tailoring each application, and answer the short questions with specific evidence instead of generic praise.
sections.body:
Applying is a skill too. Habits that turn a search into interviews:

- **Apply early** in a posting's life: with rolling review, the first weeks are best. Check target companies' pages weekly in season.
- **Tier your list**, so a tough season at the top does not leave you with nothing.
- **Tailor in five minutes**: reorder skills, pick the most relevant project, use the posting's terms.
- **Apply to the one or two roles that fit** at each company; ten unrelated applications look unfocused.
- **Keep a weekly rhythm**, noting which resume version went where.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Answer filter fields (graduation date, GPA, location, work authorization) exactly. And apply when you meet most core requirements: intern postings are often wish lists.

visual.title: Spread applications across three tiers
rows: A famous tech company with thousands of applicants
A mid-size software company that matches your skills
A local hospital's software team with few applicants

visual.title: "Why are you interested in this role?"

items.title: Generic
points: "I'm passionate about technology, and your company is a leader in the industry."
Could be pasted into any form

items.title: Specific
points: "I use your app to plan group trips, and last semester I built a small sync feature with conflict handling. I want to learn how your team keeps shared data consistent."
One thing about them, one piece of your evidence, what you want to learn

visual.title: A required cover letter
rows: "Your post on moving refunds to an event queue caught my attention: I built a queue-based notification service last semester."
2. One or two pieces of evidence
"In StudyMatch, a Flask and PostgreSQL app used by 300+ students, I designed the API and cut the slowest query from 1.2 s to 80 ms."
"I'd love to bring that backend work to your team. Thank you for your time."
visual.caption: Well under a page. When optional, a short, specific letter helps at small companies where a person reads every application; a generic one adds nothing.

sections.tip: Keep a document of your best short answers ("why this role", "a project you are proud of", "a challenge you overcame") and adapt them. Many forms ask the same few questions.
sections.pitfall: Waiting to apply until you match every requirement. Intern postings often list more than any student has; if you meet most of the core ones, apply.

check.question: An application form asks, "Why are you interested in this role?" in a small text box. Which answer is strongest?
choices: "I am passionate about technology and want to grow my skills at a leading company."
A pasted one-page cover letter
"I use your app to split rent, and I built a small payments API with idempotent requests last semester; I want to learn how your team keeps transfers reliable at scale."
"I need an internship for my degree requirements."
check.explanation: It is specific to this company, links to the applicant's own evidence and says what they want to learn, in three short lines. The first could be sent to any company, a full letter ignores the box's purpose, and the last is only about the applicant's needs.

sections.title: Referrals and networking without being awkward
sections.key: Network by asking warm connections for advice, not jobs; raise a referral only after a real conversation, and make it easy to give.
sections.body:
A **referral** means an employee submits your application internally or flags it to a recruiter. A referred application usually gets a closer look from a person instead of waiting in a large pile. It does not guarantee an interview, but few things change your odds as much.

Networking feels slimy when you picture asking strangers for jobs. Done well, it is just talking to people about work you are interested in:

[[visual]]

Good questions: What does a normal week look like on your team? What did your intern project involve? What do you wish you had known? End with **"Is there anyone else you think I should talk to?"** It turns one conversation into two.

[[visual 2]]

Give back: tell them how it turned out, share your notes with classmates, and refer others when you can.

steps.label: Find a warm connection
steps.detail: Alumni, former classmates, TAs, people from your clubs or jobs: a shared connection makes a reply far more likely

steps.label: Ask for advice, not a job
steps.detail: A 15 to 20 minute chat, or a few questions by message

steps.label: Have the conversation
steps.detail: Come prepared, ask about their work, finish on time

steps.label: If a role fits, ask whether they'd be comfortable referring you
steps.detail: Only after a real conversation, with an easy no. Many offer first

visual.title: Make referring you easy
rows: The job title, link and requisition ID
So they refer you to the right role
"Jordan is a CS junior at State who built StudyMatch, a Flask and PostgreSQL app used by 300+ students. Strong in Python and API design, interested in backend systems."

sections.tip: Keep a short list of people you have talked to and when. A note every few months ("I took your advice and built X") keeps the relationship alive without asking for anything.
sections.pitfall: Asking a stranger for a referral in your first message. It asks them to vouch for someone they know nothing about, and most will simply not reply.

check.question: An alumna replied to your message, and you had a helpful 20-minute call about her team. What's the best next step?
choices: Ask her right away to refer you to three different roles
Never contact her again so you don't seem pushy
Connect with her on every social network you can find
Thank her the same day; if a role fits, ask whether she'd be comfortable referring you and send the link, your resume and a short blurb
check.explanation: A prompt thank-you keeps the relationship good, and a single, specific referral request with everything she needs makes it easy to say yes. Asking for three roles at once overreaches, and disappearing wastes a real connection.

sections.title: Cold messages that work
sections.key: A cold message that gets answered is under about 100 words: who you are, why them specifically, one small ask, and an easy out.
sections.body:
Most cold messages fail for three reasons: too long, all about the sender, and a big ask at the end. One that works reads on a phone in ten seconds and is easy to say yes to:

[[visual]]

Keep it **under about 100 words**, with no attachments and no life story. On LinkedIn, connection notes are short and free accounts get few personalized ones, so save them for people you really want to reach; an alumni directory or a mutual friend's introduction beats a cold note.

[[visual 2]]

At startups, offer something concrete: a bug you found and wrote up, a small fix, thoughtful product feedback. It shows the skill they would hire you for. Follow up **once**, about a week later, then let it go: silence is not personal.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Anatomy of a cold message
rows: Who you are, in one line
Shows you are not mass-messaging; earns the reply
"I saw you interned on the Maps team."
Makes it easy to say yes
"Would you have 15 minutes for a call?"

items.title: Ignored
points: "Hello Sir/Madam, I am a hardworking, passionate student who has loved computers since I was young. I have attached my resume. Please refer me to any openings at your esteemed company."
No reason for choosing them, an attachment, a big ask from a stranger

items.title: Answered
points: "Hi Priya, I'm a CS junior at State and saw you interned on the Maps team before joining full time. I'm applying for SWE internships this fall and would love to hear what your intern project was like. Would you have 15 minutes for a call in the next couple of weeks? No worries if you're busy. Thanks, Jordan"

visual.title: More templates
rows: After a call, asking for a referral

"Thanks again for the call last week. Your advice paid off: I added a test suite to StudyMatch. The SWE Intern role on the Maps team (ID 12345) looks like a strong fit. Would you be comfortable referring me? Totally fine if not."
A recruiter from a career fair
"We spoke at the State career fair on Tuesday about the backend internship. I've applied (ID 12345) and wanted to say thanks for your time."
"Our club uses your sign-up tool, and the CSV export drops accented names. Here is a short reproduction. Is your team hiring interns this year? Either way, hope it helps."
"Just floating this back up in case it got buried. Totally fine if now isn't a good time. Thanks!"

sections.tip: Before sending, delete every sentence about you that they don't need in order to say yes. What remains is usually the right length.
sections.pitfall: Sending the same generic paragraph to 200 people. Without a specific reason you chose them, it reads as spam and gets ignored.

activity.title: Check a cold message
activity.prompt: Run the checker on this weak first message and read what it flags. Rewrite it in the style of template 1 (who you are, why them, one small ask, an easy out) until every line says OK, then check a message you are about to send.

props.code:
message = """Hello Sir/Madam, my name is Jordan and I am a
hardworking, passionate student who has loved computers since
I was young. I have attached my resume. Please refer me to any
openings at your esteemed company."""

EASY_OUTS = ["no worries", "totally fine", "no pressure",
             "if you're busy"]
text = message.lower()
words = len(message.split())
print(words, "words:", "OK" if words <= 100 else "aim for under 100")
checks = [
    ("asks one clear question", "?" in message),
    ("offers an easy out", any(p in text for p in EASY_OUTS)),
    ("no attachment in a first message", "attach" not in text),
    ("no referral request to a stranger", "refer" not in text),
    ("addresses a real person",
     "sir/madam" not in text and "whom" not in text),
]
for label, ok in checks:
    print("OK " if ok else "FIX", label)
print("Not checked: a specific reason you chose them. Is it there?")
props.task: Rewrite the message until every check prints OK.

check.question: Which first message to a stranger at a company is most likely to get a reply?
choices: A 400-word introduction with your resume attached
Three sentences: you're a CS junior at State, you saw their talk on the payments migration, and could they spare 15 minutes for two questions, no worries if not
"Can you refer me? Resume attached."
A message that just says "Hi" to start a conversation
check.explanation: It is short, gives a specific reason for choosing this person, makes one small ask and offers an easy out. The long version gets skimmed or skipped, the referral request asks too much of a stranger, and a bare "Hi" makes them do all the work.

sections.title: Tracking applications and handling rejection
sections.key: Track every application in a simple spreadsheet, use the numbers to find and fix your weakest stage, and treat rejection as data rather than a verdict.
sections.body:
By October you have applied to 45 companies, messaged 20 people and have three online assessments due. Without a tracker, deadlines slip, follow-ups are forgotten, and you cannot tell what works. A spreadsheet is enough:

[[visual]]

Track stages (applied, OA, phone screen, final round, offer, rejected or no response after about four weeks) and review weekly: update stages, send due follow-ups, add new applications.

The tracker shows where your search leaks, so you fix the right thing:

[[visual 2]]

Rejection is part of the process for everyone. Treat each one as data: write down the questions and where you struggled, and turn the misses into practice. Many companies share no feedback, so your notes are your feedback, and many let you reapply after 6 to 12 months.

Set goals you control: applications, messages and problems practiced each week.

visual.title: A tracker
visual.caption: Also useful: role, link, date applied, contact and notes.

visual.title: Read your numbers
rows: The resume, applying earlier, better-matched roles and more referrals
Timed practice with the pattern packs and challenges
Failing phone screens or final rounds
Mock interviews that simulate the full loop, behavioral questions included, plus notes from each round
visual.caption: Response rate = responses / applications: 6 interviews from 80 applications is 7.5%.

sections.tip: Do a 30-minute review on the same day every week. Small, regular updates beat a frantic catch-up when three OAs are due at once.
sections.pitfall: Changing everything after one rejection. A single outcome is noise; look at the pattern across your tracker before rewriting your resume or switching strategy.

activity.title: Find where your search leaks
activity.prompt: Run the summary of 30 sample applications. Which stage loses the most people, and which source gets more responses? Decide what you would fix first. Then replace the sample data with your own applications and run it again.

props.code:
# Each application: (source, furthest stage it reached)
apps = (
    [("job board", "applied")] * 20
    + [("job board", "oa")] * 2
    + [("job board", "phone")] * 2
    + [("referral", "applied")] * 1
    + [("referral", "oa")] * 1
    + [("referral", "phone")] * 1
    + [("referral", "final")] * 2
    + [("referral", "offer")] * 1
)

STAGES = ["applied", "oa", "phone", "final", "offer"]

def reached(stage):
    i = STAGES.index(stage)
    return [a for a in apps if STAGES.index(a[1]) >= i]

prev = None
for stage in STAGES:
    n = len(reached(stage))
    if prev:
        pct = round(100 * n / prev)
        print(f"{stage:8}{n:3}   {pct}% of the stage before")
    else:
        print(f"{stage:8}{n:3}")
    prev = n

print()
for source in sorted({s for s, _ in apps}):
    mine = [a for a in apps if a[0] == source]
    heard = [a for a in mine if a[1] != "applied"]
    pct = round(100 * len(heard) / len(mine))
    print(f"{source}: {len(heard)} of {len(mine)} got a response ({pct}%)")
props.task: Find the weakest stage, then swap in your own application data.

check.question: Your tracker shows 60 applications, 3 responses, and you passed 2 of those 3 phone screens. What should you work on first?
choices: Interview skills, since that is where offers are decided
Nothing; keep going exactly as you are
The application stage: the resume, applying earlier, better-matched roles and more referrals
Applying only to more famous companies
check.explanation: A 5 percent response rate is the bottleneck, while 2 of 3 phone screens passed means interviewing is going fine. Fixing the stage that loses the most people gives the biggest gain. More famous companies would make the response rate worse.

sections.title: Offers, deadlines and negotiation basics
sections.key: Get offers in writing, ask politely for more time instead of accepting and reneging, and negotiate the parts that flex, with a competing offer as your strongest lever.
sections.body:
An offer usually arrives as a recruiter's call or email, then a written offer letter. Read the details before you celebrate:

[[visual]]

If a recruiter calls with a verbal offer, thank them warmly, ask when the written offer arrives and what the deadline is, and decide from the written details. Then:

[[visual 2]]

Intern pay is often fixed by the program, especially at large companies, but other parts flex. **A competing offer is the strongest lever**, mentioned politely and specifically. Asking politely almost never gets an offer pulled at a reputable company.

[[visual 3]]

**Reneging** (backing out after accepting) burns bridges with the company and the recruiters who vouched for you, and some universities forbid it. Decide before you accept. When comparing, look past the hourly rate: housing, mentorship, what you will build and return-offer rates.

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Read the offer
rows: Usually hourly or monthly for interns
A stipend, company housing, a relocation payment, or nothing
Start and end, office or remote, the team (sometimes assigned later)
How long you have to accept; a very short one is an "exploding offer"

steps.label: Thank the recruiter; ask for the written offer and the deadline
Compare it with your other offers and processes
steps.detail: Tell other companies you have an offer with a deadline: they may speed up

steps.label: Ask for an extension or flexibility if you need it
Withdraw from your other interview processes

items.title: Often fixed
points: Intern pay, especially at large companies

visual.title: Polite, specific scripts
rows: "Thank you again for the offer; I'm very excited about the team. I'm finishing two other interview processes and want to give you a firm answer. Would it be possible to have until November 15 to decide?"
"Your team is my first choice. Another offer I have includes housing support. Is there any flexibility on the housing stipend or the start date?"

sections.tip: Ask the recruiter how often interns on the team receive return offers. Turning an internship into a full-time offer is one of the biggest wins of a good summer.
sections.pitfall: Accepting an offer just to feel safe, then reneging when a better one arrives. Ask for a deadline extension before accepting instead.

check.question: You have an offer due Friday and a final round elsewhere next Wednesday. What's the best move?
choices: Politely ask the first company for an extension, and tell the second company you have an offer with a deadline
Accept now and back out later if the other company says yes
Let the deadline pass without replying
Ask for double the pay so you have a reason to decline
check.explanation: Asking for more time is normal and often granted, and telling the other company about your deadline may speed them up. Accepting with a plan to renege burns bridges, and ignoring a deadline can lose the offer.

sections.title: Your first weeks, and earning a return offer
sections.key: Ship something small early, ask good questions after a set time, ask for feedback at the midpoint, and finish a useful, well-scoped project to earn a return offer.
sections.body:
You got the internship. The first month sets the tone, and the habits that matter are simple:

[[visual]]

When stuck, try alone for a set time (many teams suggest 15 to 30 minutes, longer for big tasks), then ask with what you are doing, what you tried and your best guess. Batch questions that are not urgent. Two days stuck in silence is far worse than asking.

[[visual 2]]

Make your work visible with short done, next, blocked updates, and meet people: teammates and other interns become references, referrals and friends.

**Earning a return offer** usually depends on three things: your project delivered something useful, how you worked with the team, and how much you grew. Ask early how interns are evaluated, agree on milestones, and **cut scope early**: a finished, tested, documented smaller project beats an ambitious half-finished one.

visual.title: Milestones
rows: Set up your environment (days is normal at a large company) and start a work log: commands, owners, acronyms, links
Meet your manager and mentor: what success looks like, how often you meet, how they like questions
Ship a small change (a docs fix, a tiny bug, a missing test) to walk branch, review, CI, merge and deploy once
Ask for specific feedback: what is going well and what to change. Behind schedule? Say so now and propose a smaller scope
Present your project from your log and measured results; hand off unfinished work; ask how return offers work and when you will hear
Update your resume while the numbers are fresh, thank your manager and mentor, connect with teammates, ask about references

items.title: Weak question
points: "The build doesn't work. Can you help?"

items.title: Strong question
points: "I'm trying to run the payments service locally. `make dev` fails with 'connection refused' on port 5432. Docker is running and I followed the setup doc through step 4. I think the database container isn't starting. Is there a step I'm missing, or someone who owns this setup?"

sections.tip: End each day with three lines in your log: what you did, what you learned, what's next. Ten minutes a day saves hours when it's time for reviews.
sections.pitfall: Staying stuck for days to avoid looking inexperienced. Interns are expected to ask; spinning in silence is what actually worries managers.

check.question: You've been stuck on a setup error for 40 minutes and have tried the obvious fixes. What's the best next step?
choices: Keep trying alone for the rest of the week so you don't bother anyone
Post "it's broken" in the whole engineering channel
Ask your mentor, giving what you're trying to do, the exact error, what you tried and your best guess
Skip the setup and write code without running anything
check.explanation: After a fair attempt, a specific question gets you unstuck fast and shows good judgment. Days of silent struggle waste the internship, and a vague post in a big channel makes others do the work of figuring out what you mean.

keyTerms.definition: Applications are reviewed as they arrive, so spots can fill before the posting closes.
An internship during the fall or spring term instead of the summer.
A longer work term, often four to eight months, built into some university programs.
An employee submitting or flagging your application internally.
A short conversation to learn about someone's work, not to ask for a job.
A first message to someone you have no prior contact with.
The share of applications that lead to any next step, such as an OA or interview.
An offer for another internship or a full-time job, made to an intern at the end of the summer.
Backing out of an offer after accepting it; it damages your reputation with that company.
A running record of what you did, learned and decided during an internship.
An offer with a very short deadline, which you can politely ask to extend.
Your list of companies to apply to, mixed across reach, target and likely tiers.

summary: Large US companies open applications in late summer and fall the year before; smaller ones hire into spring.
Search widely, verify postings, avoid scams, and apply early to a tiered list.
Ask for advice, not jobs; raise referrals after a real conversation and make them easy.
Cold messages: under about 100 words, why them, one small ask, an easy out.
Track every application and fix your weakest stage; rejection is data.
Get offers in writing, ask for extensions instead of reneging, and finish useful work to earn a return offer.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a first-year student how to land a summer internship: when to apply, where to look, how to get a referral without being awkward, and how to tell from their own numbers what to fix.

questions.question: Roughly when do applications typically open for US summer internships at large companies?
choices: A week or two before the summer starts
In March of the same year
In late summer and early fall of the year before
About two years ahead
questions.explanation: Large employers typically open summer internship applications in late summer and early fall of the previous year and fill spots on a rolling basis. Startups and smaller companies tend to hire closer to the start date, in winter and spring.

questions.question: Put the steps of a typical summer internship search in order.
items: Polish your resume and projects the summer before
Apply as large-company postings open in early fall
Take online assessments and interviews through the fall
Receive offers with decision deadlines
Keep applying to startups and mid-size companies in spring
questions.explanation: Preparation comes before postings open, the large-company wave runs through fall, and the second wave of smaller employers continues into spring.

questions.question: A posting says applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. What does that mean for you?
choices: Applications are reviewed as they arrive and spots can fill before the posting closes, so apply early
Every application is reviewed after the deadline, so timing doesn't matter
The company only interviews referred candidates
Unsuccessful applications roll over to next year automatically
questions.explanation: With rolling review, interviews happen while the posting is still open, and the program can fill before the listed deadline. An early application competes for more open spots.

questions.question: Which are good places to find software internships? Choose all that apply.
choices: Company career pages
University career fairs and Handshake
Community-maintained GitHub internship lists
Only the five most famous tech companies
Banks, hospitals and government agencies that hire software interns
questions.explanation: Career pages, university channels, community lists and less obvious employers all lead to real roles. Limiting yourself to five famous companies means competing for the most contested spots only.

questions.question: Why apply to mid-size, non-tech and local companies, not just famous tech firms?
choices: They never interview candidates
They don't ask for resumes
Famous companies don't hire interns
They get far fewer applicants per spot and still offer real engineering work
questions.explanation: Every bank, hospital and retailer runs software. Their internships are real engineering experience, and with fewer applicants your odds are much better, which matters most for a first internship.

questions.question: You sent 80 applications and got 6 interview invitations. What is your response rate as a percentage? Number only.
questions.explanation: 6 / 80 = 0.075, which is 7.5 percent. Tracking this number tells you whether to work on the application stage (resume, timing, referrals) or on interviewing.

questions.question: What is a referral, and why does it help?
questions.answer: An employee submits or flags your application internally. It usually gets a person to look at your application instead of it waiting in a large pile, which raises your chance of an interview, though it doesn't guarantee one.
questions.explanation: That is why building real relationships early matters: a referral comes from someone who can honestly say something about you.

questions.question: Who is the best first person to reach out to?
choices: A random senior director at your dream company
An alumna of your school who interned on a team you're interested in
The company's CEO
Every recruiter on LinkedIn, worldwide
questions.explanation: A shared school and a directly relevant experience make a reply far more likely, and she can tell you exactly what the internship is like. Senior strangers rarely reply, and mass messages read as spam.

questions.question: Put the steps of networking toward a referral in order.
items: Find a warm connection, such as an alum or a former classmate
Send a short message asking for a 15-minute chat
Have the conversation and ask about their work
Send a thank-you the same day
If a role fits, ask whether they'd be comfortable referring you
questions.explanation: The relationship comes before the ask. By the time you mention a referral, they know who you are and why you fit.

questions.question: Someone agreed to refer you. What should you send them? Choose all that apply.
choices: The job link and requisition ID
Your resume
A two or three sentence summary they can paste into the form
Your full transcript and every project you've ever made
A list of other companies you're applying to
questions.explanation: The link, the resume and a ready-made blurb are exactly what a referral form asks for. Extra documents make them dig, and your other applications are not their concern.

questions.question: An engineer at your dream company accepted your connection request but hasn't said anything. What's the best next message?
choices: "Can you refer me to your company?"
A specific note: why you reached out to them, one or two questions about their team, and an easy out
Your resume with no message
A long message listing every reason you want to work there
questions.explanation: Accepting a request is not agreeing to vouch for you. A short, specific note with a small ask starts a real conversation, and a referral can come later once they know you.

questions.question: Match each part of a cold message to its job.

pairs.left: Who you are, in one line

pairs.right: Makes it easy to say yes
Removes pressure to reply a certain way

questions.explanation: Each part removes a reason to ignore the message: confusion about who you are, suspicion of spam, an ask that is too big, or the awkwardness of saying no.

questions.question: What is the biggest problem with this first message to a stranger?
questions.code:
Hello Sir/Madam,

My name is Jordan and I am a hardworking, passionate student who has
loved computers since I was young. I have attached my resume, transcript
and portfolio. I am looking for an internship at your esteemed company.
Please let me know of any openings and refer me.

Regards
choices: It should also include a phone number
It should be longer so it covers the sender's whole background
It should go to more people at once
It's generic and all about the sender: no reason for choosing this person, attachments up front, and a big ask from a stranger
questions.explanation: Nothing in it shows why this person, the attachments ask them to do homework, and a referral is too big an ask for a first contact. A short, specific note with one small ask would do far better.

questions.question: About how long should a first cold message be?
choices: Under about 100 words: who you are, why them and one small ask
One line: "Refer me?"
A full page, so they know everything about you
Long enough to paste in your whole resume
questions.explanation: Short enough to read on a phone in ten seconds, but with enough context (who, why them, what you're asking) for a yes. A one-liner skips the context; a page won't get read.

questions.question: A week after your message there's no reply. What should you do?
choices: Message them every day until they answer
Message their manager instead
Send one short, polite follow-up, and let it go if there's still no reply
Post publicly that they ignored you
questions.explanation: Messages get buried, so one gentle nudge is reasonable and often works. After that, silence means busy, not rude, and pushing harder only hurts your reputation.

questions.question: Which columns belong in an application tracker? Choose all that apply.
choices: Date applied
Source (referral, career page, fair)
Current stage
Next action and its due date
Your GPA
questions.explanation: Dates, sources and stages let you see what is working, and next actions keep follow-ups and deadlines from slipping. Your GPA is the same for every row, so it tells you nothing.

questions.question: You pass most online assessments and phone screens but rarely get past final rounds. What should you focus on?
choices: Rewriting your resume from scratch
Applying to twice as many companies
Mock interviews that simulate a full loop, including behavioral questions, plus notes from each final round
Stopping algorithm practice entirely
questions.explanation: Your resume and early rounds are working; the leak is at the final stage. Full-loop mock interviews and honest notes on each final round target exactly that.

questions.question: You were rejected after a final round in October. What is the most useful response?
choices: Write down the questions and where you struggled, turn the gaps into practice, and note when you can reapply (often 6 to 12 months)
Reapply to the same role the following week
Email the interviewers to argue the decision
Decide you're not cut out for software
questions.explanation: Companies often won't share feedback, so your notes are the feedback. Many have a waiting period before you can reapply to the same role, so a no now can become a yes next season.

questions.question: Why set goals like "apply to 10 roles and practice 8 problems this week" instead of "get an offer this month"?
questions.answer: Because you control the inputs but not the outcome. Process goals keep you moving and let you measure progress, while rejections, which are normal, stay outside your control.
questions.explanation: Outcome goals swing with luck and timing and are discouraging when they slip. Process goals are what actually produce offers over a season.

questions.question: Which is the best way to ask for more time on an offer?
choices: "I need more time."
"Other companies are better, so give me more time."
Not replying until you've decided
"I'm very excited about this offer. I'm finishing a couple of other processes; would it be possible to have until November 15 to decide?"
questions.explanation: It shows enthusiasm, gives an honest reason and asks for a specific date, which is easy for a recruiter to approve. The others are vague, insulting or risk losing the offer.

questions.question: Intern pay at a large company is often fixed. Which are frequently still negotiable? Choose all that apply.
choices: Start date
The decision deadline
Team or location preference
Relocation or housing support
The program's length for every intern
questions.explanation: Recruiters often have room on individual dates, deadlines, placement and relocation even when the pay band is set. The overall program structure applies to the whole intern class and is not changed for one person.

questions.question: You accepted Company A's offer in November. In January, Company B offers more. What should you know?
choices: Reneging has no consequences for interns
Reneging burns bridges with A and the recruiters who vouched for you, and some schools have policies against it; the time to compare was before accepting
Company A will automatically match the new offer
You can accept both and decide in May
questions.explanation: An acceptance is a commitment the company plans around. Backing out damages your reputation with that company and sometimes with your school. Use extensions and timing to compare offers before you accept.

questions.question: What is usually the strongest lever in an intern offer negotiation?
choices: Saying that you need more money
A competing offer, mentioned politely and specifically
Threatening to post a bad review
Asking the same question repeatedly
questions.explanation: A real competing offer gives the recruiter a concrete reason to adjust what they can (often housing, dates or a deadline). Pressure tactics damage the relationship and rarely work.

questions.question: Put these internship milestones in the order they should happen.
items: Set up your development environment and start a work log
Meet your manager to agree on what success looks like
Ship a small change through review, CI and deploy
Ask for feedback around the midpoint
Present your project and its results at the end
questions.explanation: Setup and expectations come first, a small early change teaches the workflow, midpoint feedback leaves time to improve, and the final presentation draws on your log and results.

questions.question: Which question to your mentor is best?
choices: "The build doesn't work. Can you help?"
"Can you just fix my environment?"
"Is it normal that nothing works here?"
"`make dev` fails with 'connection refused' on port 5432. Docker is running and I followed the setup doc through step 4. I think the database container isn't starting. Am I missing a step?"
questions.explanation: It gives the goal, the exact error, what was tried and a hypothesis, so the mentor can help in a minute. The others make the mentor start from zero.

questions.question: Why aim to ship a small change in your first week or two?
choices: It walks you through the whole path (branch, review, CI, merge, deploy) once, so your real project is less mysterious
It impresses people with lines of code
It lets you skip code review later
Interns are required to deploy something on day one
questions.explanation: The first change is about learning the workflow, not the size of the change. Once you've been through review and deployment, your main project only has the hard parts left.

questions.question: Halfway through your internship, your manager hasn't said how you're doing. What should you do?
choices: Wait for the final review, then react
Assume everything is fine
Ask for specific feedback now: what's going well and what to change in the second half
Ask the other interns how they think you're doing
questions.explanation: Midpoint feedback is when it is still useful: you have weeks left to act on it, which can decide a return offer. Waiting until the end turns feedback into a verdict.

questions.question: What helps most at a university career fair?
choices: Collecting a bag of free items from every booth
Handing over your resume without speaking
A 30-second pitch, a few printed resumes and a specific question for each company you visit
Only visiting the booth with the longest line
questions.explanation: Recruiters remember a clear pitch and a thoughtful question, and a printed resume gives them something to note on. Going early in the day, before lines and fatigue build up, helps too.

questions.question: You are an international student in the US and want a summer internship. What should you do early in your search?
choices: Talk to your school's international student office about work authorization, such as CPT, and answer form questions accurately
Ignore authorization questions on forms; they are optional
Wait until you have an offer before learning the rules
Apply only to remote roles, which need no authorization
questions.explanation: Work authorization rules decide which internships you can accept and when. Your school's international student office handles this (F-1 students commonly use Curricular Practical Training), and forms ask about authorization, so you need accurate answers.

questions.question: Which are warning signs of an internship scam? Choose all that apply.
choices: You must pay for training or equipment before starting
They send a check to deposit and ask you to send part of it back
You are hired after a text-only chat with no real interview
The same posting appears on the company's own careers site
A recruiter schedules a video call to discuss the role
questions.explanation: Real employers do not charge you for equipment or training, do not ask you to deposit a check and send money back, and do not hire after a text-only chat. A posting that also appears on the company's own careers site is a good sign, not a warning.

questions.question: A posting lists eight requirements for interns, and you meet five of the core ones. What should you do?
choices: Skip it, since you do not meet every requirement
Apply, leading with the evidence that matches the core requirements
Add the missing skills to your resume anyway
Email the recruiter asking whether you should apply
questions.explanation: Intern requirement lists are often wish lists, and nobody expects a student to have everything. If you meet most of the core requirements, apply and lead with the evidence that matches.

questions.question: A posting requires a cover letter. Which structure works best?
choices: Two pages about your life story
A restatement of your resume, line by line
A generic letter you send to every company
Three short paragraphs: why this company and role, one or two pieces of evidence, a brief close
questions.explanation: Three short paragraphs keep it readable: a specific reason for this company and role, one or two pieces of evidence, and a brief close. A long life story or a generic letter adds nothing a reviewer can use.

questions.question: You find eight open roles at one company, including data science, frontend, mobile and security internships. What is the best approach?
choices: Apply to all eight to maximize your chances
Apply to the one or two that fit your experience, and tailor for them
Apply to the one with the fewest applicants, whatever it is
Apply to none, since you cannot choose
questions.explanation: Recruiters can see every application you submit, and scattered applications to unrelated roles look unfocused. Pick the one or two roles that genuinely match your experience and tailor for those.

questions.question: Match each tier of your target list to an example.

pairs.right: A famous tech company with thousands of applicants
A mid-size software company that matches your skills
A local hospital's software team with few applicants

questions.explanation: A tiered list spreads risk: reach companies are the most competitive, target companies fit well with realistic odds, and likely companies have fewer applicants per spot.

questions.question: Which first message to an engineer at a 20-person startup is most likely to get a useful reply?
choices: "I love your company! Are you hiring? Resume attached."
"Our club uses your sign-up tool and I found that the CSV export drops accented names; here is a short reproduction. I'm looking for a summer internship; is your team hiring interns?"
"Please let me know about any openings that match my profile."
"Can we schedule an hour-long call so I can learn about your startup?"
questions.explanation: Offering something concrete (a reproduced bug in their product) shows exactly the skill they hire for and gives them a reason to reply even if they are not hiring. Generic praise, attachments and job requests ask for their time without giving anything.

questions.question: A recruiter calls with a verbal offer and asks whether you accept right now. What should you do?
choices: Accept immediately so they do not change their mind
Decline, because good offers are always in writing first
Thank them warmly, ask when the written offer will arrive and what the deadline is, and decide from the written details
Ask for double the pay before hearing the details
questions.explanation: A verbal offer is great news, but the written offer holds the details you need to decide. Thanking them, asking for the written offer and its deadline, and deciding from that is normal and expected.

questions.question: Put the steps for handling an offer in order.
items: Thank the recruiter and ask for the written offer and deadline
Compare the details with any other offers or processes
Ask for an extension or flexibility if you need it
Accept in writing
Withdraw from your other interview processes
questions.explanation: Get the details and deadline in writing, compare them, ask for any extension or flexibility before you commit, then accept in writing and withdraw from other processes. Asking after you accept is too late.

questions.question: What usually matters most for an intern's return offer?
choices: The number of hours you were online
The total lines of code you wrote
Whether your project delivered something useful, how you worked with the team, and how much you grew
How many other interns you got to know
questions.explanation: Managers typically weigh whether the project delivered something useful, how the intern worked with the team and how much they grew. Hours and lines of code are poor proxies for any of that.

questions.question: Week 6 of 12: your project is behind and the original plan will not finish. What is the best move?
choices: Work nights quietly and hope to catch up
Tell your manager now, propose a smaller scope you can finish well, and agree on it
Wait until the final presentation to explain the delay
Switch to a different project without telling anyone
questions.explanation: Raising it early and agreeing on a smaller, finished scope is what managers want to see. A tested, documented smaller project usually reads better than an ambitious half-finished one, and hiding the problem until the end removes every option.

questions.question: What should you do in the week after your internship ends?
questions.answer: Update your resume with specific bullets and numbers while they are fresh, thank your manager and mentor, connect with teammates on LinkedIn, and ask whether they would be a reference.
questions.explanation: The details and numbers fade fast, and the people you worked with are your best references and referral sources for the next step.

questions.question: Your 15-minute informational chat is ending. Which closing question is most useful?
choices: "Can you get me an interview?"
"Is there anyone else you think I should talk to?"
"How much do you earn?"
"Can we make this an hour next time?"
questions.explanation: Asking who else to talk to turns one conversation into more, without asking for anything they would find awkward. Asking for a job or a referral at this point skips the relationship.
